title: Is It Worth Your Budget? AI Detection Software
author: RatedEd
summary: RatedEd runs the arithmetic school leaders rarely see in a vendor demo: even a 1 percent false-positive rate on an AI-detection tool means a single 60-teacher building could falsely accuse roughly 144 students of cheating every year. Reviewing the peer-reviewed evidence, including the widely cited Stanford finding that detectors misfire on non-native English writers at rates over 60 percent, the piece rates Turnitin, GPTZero, and Pangram, concluding none has independently verified accuracy good enough to justify the liability, and that 'buying nothing' while redesigning assignments around visible process (drafts, version history, in-class writing) is the actual best-value option. It closes with four questions administrators should ask before adopting any detector and a recommendation that a flagged score should trigger a conversation, never an automatic penalty.
points: Runs the false-positive math: a 1 percent error rate across 240 papers a year per teacher produces real, wrongly accused students at scale.
Summarizes the Stanford Patterns study showing detectors misclassify non-native English writers at rates as high as 61 percent, and traces vendor rebuttals.
Rates Turnitin, GPTZero, and Pangram, finding self-reported vendor numbers are the weakest link in the evidence.
Recommends process-based assignment design (drafts, version history, in-class writing, specific local prompts) as the free alternative that survives every model release.
quotes: Take a detector with a 1 percent false positive rate, an optimistic figure. Now run your building. Thirty students, eight writing assignments a year, one teacher. That is 240 papers. At 1 percent, that teacher falsely accuses two or three students a year.
The detectors were near-perfect on the eighth-grade essays. On the TOEFL essays they averaged a 61.22 percent false positive rate.

Most detectors score on perplexity, roughly how surprising the word choices are. Writers with a smaller working vocabulary produce more predictable prose, which reads as machine-like. So the mechanism penalizes limited linguistic range, and your multilingual learners have limited linguistic range by definition. That is not a bug someone will patch.

The margin of error is roughly plus or minus 15 percentage points, meaning a reported score of 50 could actually be anywhere from 35 to 65. Turnitin claims a false positive rate under 1 percent, while a Washington Post test on a smaller sample produced far higher rates.
Write the appeal process before you need it: a score alone never triggers a consequence, it triggers a conversation about process, not about the number.
